extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of hydrostatics / natural philosophers interested in fluid-pressure experiments
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of classical hydrostatics propositions and experiment descriptions about fluid pressures (upward, downward, lateral, oblique) and how they depend on depth/height, including layered fluids and the role of air. Intended as foundational laws and experimental demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure adapts to height/depth not to breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Thus we see every Thing adapts it self to the Heighth or Depth. ... the Breadth or Surface of the Water makes no Alteration.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated experimental demonstration: changing the breadth or surface area of the containing vessel (e.g., using a bucket or tub larger or smaller) while keeping the same vertical height yields the same upward/ downward effect in connected tubes; the pressure on a horizontal plane depends only on the perpendicular depth (height) of the fluid above it, not on the quantity or breadth of fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force on a part equals weight of its perpendicular column (Law of Altitude/Depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That the Force which presses each Part upon the other, is equal to the Weight of the perpendicular Column of the Fluid.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement of the hydrostatical proposition: two or more equal parts of a horizontal plane will each be pressed upwards and downwards with the weight of their respective perpendicular columns; used throughout as foundational — demonstrated by experiments with tubes and communicating vessels. This underlies conclusions such as equal pressure on equal areas at the same depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal parts of a horizontal plane are pressed equally
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If we suppose a stagnating Fluid ... a Number of equal Parts taken at Pleasure ... Being First press'd upwards with an equal Force: And Secondly, downwards, with one and the same Force as another ...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any equal parts (areas) of the same horizontal plane in a connected fluid receive equal upward and downward pressures provided they are at the same level and in communication. Experimental support: communicating tubes and equal rise of liquid to same height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of an upward pressure in fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘That in Water and other Fluids a Pressure upwards has likewise Place, may be inferred from many Water-Works and Fountains that throw up Water.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments: stopping a tube with a finger and thrusting it down into water causes the internal air/water to be driven against the finger when released; when the finger is removed water often rises above the external surface and oscillates before settling — demonstrating a real upward acting force. Further demonstrations include placing a light lid over a tube or using curved tubes to show suspension effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward pressure equals weight of perpendicular column (detailed)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘vt is also prest upwards by a Force equal to the Weight of this Column of Altitude.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from equilibrium: when a parcel of fluid remains at a given point (neither rising nor falling) the upward and downward forces must be equal; downward force is weight of the column above, hence upward force equals that weight. Verified by experiments with tubes where removing a plug causes rise/fall to external level depending on comparison between upward pressure and column weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered fluids: stacked columns sum their weights (pressures from multiple fluids)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In several Fluids incumbent upon each other ... each Height ... preſſes downwards with the particular Weight of every Fluid of which it is the Height.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments described with 'pickle' (saline water), oil of turpentine, and quicksilver show that when fluids lie unmixably on one another the pressure at a given point is determined by the sum of the perpendicular depths and the weights of the stacked fluids (i.e., a column composed of the different fluids). Demonstrations: communicating tubes with layers, quicksilver shifting in one leg when tube moved between layers, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique (curved) columns exert same pressure as perpendicular column of same top height
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If a Part CD of a Horizontal Plane ... is press'd by a Curve or Oblique Column of Water CEFND; the Pressure it undergoes is neither greater nor lesser, than that of the Column of Altitude; that is, of the Perpendicular ConC GH D...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of curved/re-entrant tubes: a curved or oblique leg containing fluid that reaches up to the same upper surface produces the same pressure on the pressed part as a straight perpendicular column whose top reaches to the same surface — the geometry or 'obliquity' and the quantity of fluid in the oblique limb do not change the pressure so long as the perpendicular height is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral (horizontal) pressure depends on depth/height
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This Lateral Presure does also adapt it self to the Height ... fill the Vessel up to AB, so that there will then be a greater Depth of Water EB above the Tube EF; and you will find that the Stream FI K gushes out so much farther...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical demonstration by a horizontal side tube in a vessel: the horizontal range and velocity of the emerging jet increase with the vertical depth of fluid above the orifice; varying breadth without changing depth does not change the horizontal reach. This shows lateral thrust magnitude is a function of depth, not total volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication principle: connected parts at same horizontal level have same pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple passages (tubes) with upper orifices placed in the same horizontal plane exhibit liquid at equal heights in each tube; 'we always found that the Liquor within the Glass remain'd unchangeably at E.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments with paired tubes whose lower orifices are placed at the same horizontal plane show equal liquid heights when in communication — used repeatedly as empirical support for equal pressure on equal horizontal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air (or upper fluid) pressure influences suspended columns and inverted vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion and experiments with an inverted drinking-glass/cup and with air-pumped vessels show that the pressure of the air which gravitates upon the water is the cause that the water continues suspended in the glass at certain levels; the earlier propositions assume cases where the pressure of the air produces no remarkable alterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: many of the simple laws are stated 'when there is no other gravitating Fluid upon the Water a b ; and that the Pressure of the Air ... is only the Cause here that the Water continues suspended in the Glass.' The text therefore separates idealized cases (neglecting air) from practical ones where atmospheric pressure matters; experiments with inverted glasses and air-pumps illustrate the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatical paradox / independence of base force from vessel shape
rubrics_metrics.description: Through repeated experiments and the 'Law of Altitude' it is shown that 'one of these Parts, such as AB, is press'd downwards with the same Force as another ...' regardless of the breadth of the vessel; the pressure on a base depends on the perpendicular column above it, not on the total quantity of the fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental constructions (variously-shaped vessels, communicating tubes, and measured equalities of heights and quicksilver levels) are used to demonstrate that pressure at a base or on a part equals the weight of a perpendicular column having the same base area and height — giving rise to what is now called the hydrostatic paradox. The text shows how to select an equivalent columnal representation to compute the pressure.
